chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Abu al-Fadl al-Hannat (the cloth merchant) said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'What is your trade?' I said: 'A cloth merchant, and sometimes I arrive when there is a shortage (of goods) and sometimes when there is a glut (surplus), so I hold back (my goods).' He said: 'And what do the people say about you in this regard?' I said: 'They say I am a hoarder (muhtakir).' He said: 'Does anyone else sell it (the held goods)?' I said: 'I do not sell from a thousand parts even one part.' He said: 'There is no harm. That was only a man from Quraysh, called Hakim ibn Hizam. When food entered Medina, he would buy it all. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) passed by him and said: "O Hakim ibn Hizam, beware of hoarding!"'.

key_terms.حَكِيمُ بْنُ حِزَامٍ: Hakim ibn Hizam, a companion of the Prophet known for his trade

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between permissible trade holding and prohibited hoarding (hukrah) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* to distinguish between permissible commercial speculation and the prohibited practice of *hukrah* (monopolistic hoarding). The Imam validates the merchant's practice of holding inventory during market fluctuations, citing the precedent of Hakim ibn Hizam, whose holding of foodstuffs was only cautioned against by the Prophet when it approached total market control. This establishes a nuanced Shia legal view that hoarding is not inherently sinful but becomes so when it deprives the public of essential goods or creates artificial scarcity.
